title: Cache thrashing and fallback characterization
content:
Purpose:
This working note documents an investigation into intermittent latency spikes traced to kernel fallback and cache thrashing during mixed-length attention workloads. The goal is to 1) reproduce with minimal harness, 2) collect deterministic traces and perf counters, 3) test mitigations (warmup, soft-eviction, batch coalescing), and 4) propose a short-term patch and a long-term scheduler change.

High-level hypothesis:
- Under mixed short+long sequences, the KV cache occupancy and eviction patterns cause repeated demotion from fused/Flash-like kernels to a paged/emulated attention path. That demotion is expensive: extra memory copies and kernel reinitialization cause 10–50 ms microbursts. Thrashing is worse when sequence-length distribution has a heavy tail and the batch coalescer frequently assembles batches with divergent max-seq.

Repro recipe (minimal harness):
- Binary: serving-runtime/device_bench (dev build w/trace macros enabled)
- Model: 2-layer, GPT-like toy (d_model=1024, n_heads=16) converted with same kernel selection metadata as prod models
- Input generator: mix-r: for i in 1..N generate token_len = if rand() < p_tail then long_len else short_len
- Params: N=10000, p_tail=0.03, short_len=8, long_len=1024, batch_size_target=32, kv_cache_capacity=128kB/chunk (runtime override)
- Command: ./device_bench --mix-r --p 0.03 --short 8 --long 1024 --batches 312 --trace=/tmp/trace.pb

Signals captured:
- Kernel selection logs (timestamped): which kernel chosen per request (fused/flash/paged/naive)
- NVTX regions and wall-clock latency
- Per-kernel SM utilization and achieved TFLOPS (NVIDIA CUPTI counters)
- GPU DRAM bandwidth usage (NVIDIA SMI sampling)
- KV cache hit/miss counters and eviction counts
- Host<->device memcpy sizes and times

Repro results summary:
- Observed microbursts of 18–42 ms every ~250–800ms in mixed runs.
- Kernel logs show a pattern: repeated switch from fused/Flash path to paged attention when a long request is injected, then a sequence of 6–12 subsequent short requests still routed to fallback due to cache state.
- KV cache eviction spikes correlate with memcpy spikes of ~2.6MB per request during fallback warmup.
- CUPTI traces show kernel launch stalls (200–500us) while allocator/priming routines run.
- Baseline: all-short workload steady p95 ~6ms. Mixed tail workload p95 spikes 45ms.

Micro-investigations performed:
1) Warmup on long request only once per epoch
   - Approach: for batches containing a long request, call flashinit() once, mark keyed state as primed.
   - Result: reduced fallbacks by ~60%, p95 spikes reduced to 18–22ms.
   - Caveat: requires consistent tagging and can leak primed state between customers if not scoped.

2) Soft-eviction policy (LRU with hysteresis)
   - Approach: change eviction threshold to keep small frequent entries pinned and evict larger blocks only when free < 20%.
   - Result: reduced memcpy churn, but tail for extreme long bursts still triggered fallback. Throughput improved by 8% for mixed flows.

3) Batch-coalescer conservative mode
   - Approach: allocate max-seq per-cohort and avoid mixing lengths in same CUDA stream; prefer splitting a batch into two streams for clearer kernel affinity.
   - Result: avoided many cross-request kernel switches, but increased overall GPU active time by ~6% (worse utilization) — better latency SLOs.

4) Prefetch/async-prepare path
   - Approach: when a long request is enqueued, asynchronously prepare its priming buffers on a low-priority stream to overlap with earlier short requests.
   - Result: effective when prefetch completes before eviction threshold; reduced p95 spikes in 70% of attempts. Complexity: needs robust stream synchronization and backpressure awareness.

Low-level profile snapshot (example trace extract):
- t=3452.11ms request A (short) -> fused kernel chosen -> exec 4.9ms
- t=3498.33ms request B (long) -> fallback paged path -> memcpy 2.7MB, priming kernels run -> exec 26.4ms
- t=3525.08ms request C (short) -> observed goto fallback (cache cold) -> memcpy 2.6MB -> exec 18.9ms
- NVTX: many small host->device copies concurrent with kernel launches; queueing delays observed in stream 0.

Root-cause candidates: 
- KV cache allocator is size-agnostic: allocating large shadow buffers for long sequences forces eviction of many small entries, causing immediate warmup on subsequent small sequences.
- Kernel handshake path recompiles/changes state when key metadata differs (max-kv-length) causing stalls.
- Batch coalescer mixes raw sequences into same CUDA stream leading to kernel rebinds and stream serialization.

Short-term mitigations (ship in patch release):
- Add conservative batcher flag (--no-mix-large) to avoid mixing long sequences with short ones on same stream by default. Fast toggle via runtime config.
- Add soft-eviction hysteresis with conservative default thresholds and per-tenant scoping (so state doesn't leak across customers).
- Add an async priming hook (disabled by default) to preallocate priming buffers when a long request is enqueued. Requires opt-in until stable.

Long-term proposals (architecture):
- Per-cohort KV arenas: allocate per-length-range arenas so large allocations do not evict small ones.
- Kernel selection fast-path: a small metadata fingerprint to avoid heavy handshake when switching between compatible kernels (reduces 200–500us stalls).
- Scheduler-aware batching: extend batch coalescer to be aware of seq-length histograms and optimize stream assignment to minimize kernel switches while keeping high utilization.

Experiment log and next steps:
- 2025-01-12: seed hypothesis, initial harness built (Lina)
- 2025-01-15: warmup-only experiment (Marco) -> promising
- 2025-01-21: soft-eviction prototype (Priya) -> improved churn
- 2025-01-28: coalescer conservative mode A/B tests (Evan) -> latency better, utilization down
- 2025-02-03: async-prepare spikes evaluated across 3 GPU types (p4d, a10g, h100) -> variable benefit; H100 shows best overlap due to kernel concurrency.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Measure inter-tenant leakage risk for per-tenant primed state. Is KMS/HSM or tenant-id mapping enough? (Action: Security review, Priya)
- What is the memory overhead for per-cohort arenas for 99th percentile customers? (Action: Cost model, Marco)
- Add microbench for handshake path alone (no kernels) to precisely quantify the 200–500us stall components (allocator vs metadata compute). (Action: Lina)
- Test heuristics on live Dedicated pool (staging) with synthetic tail to validate safety under real traffic variety. (Action: runbook + SRE)

Attachments (inline snippets and sample graphs live in linked_artifacts):
- perf flamegraphs (link in artifacts)
- raw CUPTI capture (link in artifacts)
- minimal harness code (github link above)

Notes to reviewers:
- This is an in-progress doc intended to capture experiments and immediate mitigation options. Please add notes inline or in the PR referenced above. If you reproduce, capture nvprof/CUPTI traces and the kernel selection logs (enable --trace-kernel-choice).

Bottom line:
- Cache thrash driven fallback is a credible cause for intermittent microburst latency in mixed-length workloads. A combination of conservative batching, soft-eviction, and async priming yields immediate relief; architecture improvements (per-cohort arenas and handshake fast-path) will provide durable fixes while preserving utilization.
